Second-Generation Dacia Spring Is a Complete Revamp of an EV That Has Taken Europe by Storm
25 photos
Photo: Dacia
If one is allowed to call a vehicle low-cost, then the Dacia Spring would be the definition of that. With a price of under 18,000 euros (almost $20,000 at today’s exchange rates) and decent performance for people in the market for a small city car, the Romanian brand’s entry-level vehicle is about to become even more enticing, now that the second generation is here.
Having entered the market back in 2021 as a sort of remake of the Renault City K-ZE (Renault is Dacia’s mother company), packing a Chinese-made electric powertrain, along with body and underpinnings used on several Chinese models, the Spring proved too hard to resist for no less than 210,00 European buyers in some 40 countries.
Back in March, Dacia presented its strategy leading into the next decade, and as part of that it announced that it will release no less than four all-electric vehicles by 2030, a major change of direction for a brand that has until recently focused exclusively on internal combustion engine models.
The first of the four Romanian EVs is the second generation of the Spring, which was presented this week as the freshest offering in the A segment. As Dacia itself says, the only thing it has in common with its predecessor is the name.
Photo: Dacia For the newcomer, Dacia completely shifted direction and opted to build it on Renault's new RG-EV small platform, which is also used on the likes of the E-Tech Twingo and 5, among others. What this did, first and foremost, was to widen the body of the small four-wheeler by seven inches (18 cm).
The platform supports a new electric powertrain and an optimized battery pack. Dacia does not specifically say if this hardware is made in-house or sourced from elsewhere, but it did reveal what they are capable of.
The car's electric motor is good for 80 horsepower and 175 Nm of torque, more than enough for a small city car, and punchy enough to accelerate the Spring from zero to 62 mph in 12.1 seconds, on the way to a top speed of 81 mph (130 kph).
The motor draws power from a 27.5 kWh usable capacity LFP battery, which can store enough electricity to keep the car going for as many as 155 miles (250 km), as measured under the WLTP combined cycle. That's more than enough for the needs of people going for such a small car, which, as per Dacia's own claims, in the first-generation form, covered just 21 miles (34 km) per day on average.
Photo: Dacia As standard, the new Dacia Spring is fitted with a 6.6 kW AC onboard charger that allows the car to be plugged into a domestic socket. It's painfully slow, though, as it needs nine hours to get the Spring from 15 to 80 percent capacity.
Dacia will offer people the option of going for a heavy-duty socket, which cuts the charging times for the same interval to five hours and 40 minutes, or a seven kW wallbox that brings that even lower, at almost three hours.
Finally, there is also a fast charge solution comprising an 11 kW AC charger and 50 kW DC charger, which brings charging times down to almost two hours and 28 minutes, respectively.
There will be several trim levels on the table (Dacia hasn't detailed them all), each with its own particularities. The Journey, for instance, throws in a hands-free card, a reversing camera, and the Media Nav Live system that brings along a 10.1-inch central touchscreen and wireless smartphone mirroring via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. The Expression version, on the other hand, is equipped with a multimedia system with steering wheel controls.
Photo: Dacia No matter the trim level, the new Dacia Spring throws in a seven-inch instrument panel screen, automatic electric parking brake, and reversing sensors. There are two wheel choices on the table, coming it at 15- and 16 inches.
As for colors, the fresh bodywork of the vehicle can be had in one of four hues, Agave, Schist Grey, Diamond Black, and Glacier White, while the interior will only go for a bluish shade for the upholstery, with Agave accents here and there.
Unlike most other cars Dacia makes, which are produced in Romania, the new Dacia Spring will originate from the company's factory in Novo Mesto, Slovenia . The company did not say when we are to expect the city car to become available to customers.
Pricing for it is also a mystery at the time of writing, but not really, if you think about it. The carmaker is likely to keep the price as low as possible, as this is the only way it can fight entry-level Chinese cars, so don't be surprised if we'll still be dealing with a sticker reading under or around $20,000. We'll be on the lookout for that bit of info and let you know once we learn more.
